questions.stem: Which soil is called 'Regur' and is ideal for cotton cultivation?

options.option_text: Black soil (Regur)
Red soil
Alluvial soil
Laterite soil

questions.explanation: Black/Regur soil: rich in calcium carbonate, potash, lime. Found in Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat). Excellent moisture retention — ideal for cotton.

questions.stem: The most widespread soil type in India, found in the Indo-Gangetic Plains, is:

options.option_text: Alluvial soil
Black soil
Laterite soil
Desert soil

questions.explanation: Alluvial soil covers ~43% of India, deposited by rivers. Extremely fertile, supports most agriculture.
questions.subject: Geography

options.option_text: High iron and aluminium content, poor in nitrogen and humus
High organic matter in river deltas
High lime content in arid zones
Rich silica in semi-arid zones

questions.explanation: Laterite forms in hot, wet conditions with heavy leaching. Rich in iron oxides (red colour), poor in fertility. Found in Kerala, Karnataka, Odisha plateaus.

questions.stem: Khadar and Bhangar are two types of:

options.option_text: Alluvial soil — Khadar is newer (flood plains), Bhangar is older (uplands)
Black soil
Red soil
Desert soil

questions.explanation: Khadar = newer alluvial in flood plains, more fertile. Bhangar = older alluvial on higher ground, contains lime nodules (kankars).

questions.stem: Red soil gets its colour from:

options.option_text: Ferric oxide (iron oxide)
Carbon compounds
High clay minerals
Volcanic basalt

questions.explanation: Red soil's colour = diffuse ferric oxide. When hydrated, turns yellow. Found in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Chhattisgarh.

questions.stem: Saline/alkaline soils (Reh, Usar, Thur) are common in:

options.option_text: Semi-arid UP, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan
Northeastern hill states
Western Ghats
Andaman Islands

questions.explanation: Saline soils form where drainage is poor and evaporation high — salts accumulate. Common in UP's Bundelkhand, Haryana, Rajasthan.

questions.stem: Which soil has the highest water retention capacity?

options.option_text: Black soil (Regur)
Sandy soil
Laterite soil
Red soil

questions.explanation: Black soil swells when wet, develops cracks when dry. High clay content gives exceptional water retention.

questions.stem: Peaty and marshy soils are primarily found in:

options.option_text: Kerala backwaters, coastal Odisha, and Sundarbans
Thar Desert
Deccan Plateau
Punjab plains

questions.explanation: Peaty soils form in heavy-rainfall, poor-drainage areas with organic accumulation. Found in coastal Kerala, Odisha, Sundarbans.

questions.stem: The arid soils of western Rajasthan are distinguished by a hard, impermeable sub-surface layer locally called 'kankar'. What is kankar primarily composed of?

options.option_text: Laterite crust formed by iron and aluminium oxide accumulation
Calcium carbonate (lime) deposited by upward capillary water movement
Compacted silica and quartz grains cemented by wind-blown dust
Manganese nodules concentrated by alternating wet and dry cycles

questions.explanation: In low-rainfall arid zones, evaporation exceeds precipitation, so water moves upward by capillarity, depositing dissolved calcium carbonate at a certain depth to form the kankar layer. Laterite crust (Option A) is iron/aluminium oxide and forms in high-rainfall humid areas — the opposite of arid Rajasthan. Manganese nodules (Option D) are associated with waterlogged tropical soils, not desert profiles.

questions.stem: Mountain and forest soils found in the Himalayan foothills and the Western Ghats are generally unsuitable for intensive food-crop farming primarily because:

options.option_text: They are alkaline in pH and rich in calcium carbonate nodules
They are acidic, thin, and deficient in potassium, phosphorus, and lime
They have very high clay content causing severe waterlogging problems
They are formed on impermeable bedrock preventing any root penetration

questions.explanation: Forest/mountain soils are acidic (pH < 6) due to organic acids from decomposing leaf litter and are generally deficient in potassium, phosphorus, and lime, which limits food-crop yields. They are suitable for tea, coffee, and temperate fruits. Option A (alkaline with kankar) describes arid soils of Rajasthan. Option C is closer to black soils, which are fertile — the opposite of infertile mountain soils.

questions.stem: The clay mineral that gives black cotton soil its 'self-ploughing' property — forming deep cracks in summer and swelling shut after the first rains — belongs to which structural group?

options.option_text: Kaolinite, a 1:1 non-swelling clay typical of heavily leached soils
Montmorillonite, a 2:1 expanding lattice clay with high shrink-swell ratio
Illite, a moderately expanding clay common in alluvial plains soils
Chlorite, a non-expanding clay mineral abundant in acidic forest soils

questions.explanation: Montmorillonite (smectite group) has a 2:1 layer structure and absorbs water between its sheets, causing the soil to swell enormously on wetting and shrink dramatically on drying — producing the wide cracks and self-ploughing effect. Kaolinite (Option A) is a non-swelling 1:1 clay found in laterite soils. Illite (Option C) shows only moderate expansion and is a common distractor because it occurs in alluvial soils which are sometimes confused with black soils.

questions.stem: Which Indian state has the single largest geographical area under black cotton (regur) soils, making it the core of India's traditional cotton cultivation belt?

options.option_text: Gujarat, which has the largest share of the Rann and alluvial plains
Maharashtra, which accounts for the maximum area under Deccan Trap regur
Andhra Pradesh, where Krishna-Godavari delta black soils predominate
Madhya Pradesh, which lies entirely within the Deccan basalt lava zone

questions.explanation: Black cotton soils are derived from Deccan Trap basalts (volcanic lava flows). Maharashtra covers the largest area of the Deccan Trap and therefore has the greatest extent of regur soils, especially in Vidarbha and Marathwada. Gujarat (Saurashtra) also has black soils but covers a smaller total area. Madhya Pradesh has black soils only in its western districts — not the maximum national area. Option D's claim that MP 'lies entirely' within the Deccan Trap is factually incorrect.

questions.stem: Laterite soils require heavy fertiliser inputs before being used for food-crop farming because intense leaching depletes which pair of plant nutrients most critically?

options.option_text: Iron and Aluminium, which are washed out under heavy monsoon rainfall
Nitrogen and Phosphorus, which are rapidly lost through intense leaching
Silica and Manganese, which precipitate as insoluble oxide compounds
Potassium and Sodium, which bind firmly to 2:1 swelling clay minerals

questions.explanation: During laterisation, silica and bases are leached away while iron and aluminium oxides concentrate and remain (they are NOT leached — ruling out Option A, the most tempting distractor). The critical plant nutrients lost are Nitrogen and Phosphorus, making laterite soils infertile for most food crops. This is why tea and cashew — crops tolerant of acidic, low-nutrient conditions — are cultivated on laterites rather than wheat or rice.

questions.stem: In pedological terminology, 'illuviation' — the defining process of the B-horizon in a soil profile — refers specifically to:

options.option_text: Downward removal of fine particles and soluble material from the topsoil
Upward capillary movement of salts that form a white surface crust
Deposition of clay, humus, and iron oxides leached down from the A-horizon
In-situ weathering of parent rock that gradually transforms it into soil

questions.explanation: The B-horizon is the zone of illuviation — where materials leached (eluviated) from the A-horizon are deposited. Eluviation (Option A) is the downward washing that occurs IN the A-horizon itself; illuviation is the receiving/deposition process in the B-horizon. Option A is the most common wrong answer because candidates confuse eluviation with illuviation. Option B describes capillary rise, which creates saline soils. Option D describes the C-horizon formation from parent material.

questions.stem: Under the USDA Soil Taxonomy system adopted by India's NBSS&LUP, black cotton (regur) soils are classified as 'Vertisols'. Which diagnostic property formally places them in this order?

options.option_text: Presence of an argillic horizon with >35% clay accumulation in the subsoil
High shrink-swell clay content (≥30%) causing vertic properties year-round
Extreme iron/aluminium oxide enrichment with a lateritic (oxic) B-horizon
Thick dark mollic epipedon formed by organic matter in sub-humid grasslands

questions.explanation: In USDA Soil Taxonomy, Vertisols are defined by vertic properties — at least 30% 2:1 clay (primarily montmorillonite) that swells and shrinks seasonally, creating slickensides and pedoturbation (churning). Option A describes Alfisols (argillic horizon). Option C describes Oxisols — the classification for true tropical laterites — a common distractor since both Vertisols and Oxisols are found on the Deccan. Option D describes Mollisols of temperate grasslands (US Midwest/Ukraine), which are dark like Vertisols but form under entirely different climate and vegetation.
